title: Extension methods and C# 14 extension members
body: Extension methods add methods to existing types without modifying them. The classic form is a static method in a static class whose first parameter has `this`: `public static bool IsBlank(this string? s)`. Callers write `name.IsBlank()` once the namespace is imported. LINQ is built this way. Extensions cannot access private members and lose to an instance method with the same signature.

C# 14 adds extension blocks, a new syntax that also supports extension properties, static extension members and operators. Inside a static class, `extension(string? text) { public bool IsBlank => string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(text); }` declares an extension property used as `name.IsBlank`. The parameter in parentheses is the receiver.

A block with only a receiver type and no name, `extension(Temperature) { public static Temperature Freezing => ... }`, declares static extension members called as if they were static members of the type: `Temperature.Freezing`. Static extension operators are allowed too, so you can define `+` for a type you do not own.

Extension blocks may be generic, `extension<T>(IEnumerable<T> source)`, with constraints. The new syntax is source- and binary-compatible with classic extension methods: both can coexist and callers cannot tell them apart. C# 15 adds extension indexers (final stage).

Extensions are resolved statically from the variable's compile-time type and the imported namespaces. Check for ambiguity when two imported namespaces define the same extension, and prefer instance members when you own the type.

challenge: Add an extension block for DateOnly that provides an IsWeekend property and a static extension property DateOnly.Epoch returning 1970-01-01. Print both for 2026-10-17.
question: What does an `extension(Temperature) { public static ... }` block without a parameter name declare?
correct: Static extension members called like Temperature.Member
wrong: Instance extension methods with an implicit this
reasoning: A receiver-type-only block extends the type itself; a named receiver declares instance-style members.
